newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austrian chancellor condemns latest bomb attack.
newsitem.headline: Austrian chancellor condemns latest bomb attack.

text.p: Chancellor Franz Vranitzky on Tuesday condemned a fresh letter bomb attack in Austria as an assault on democracy but a former Vienna mayor blamed the government for failing to do enough to hunt down the bombers.
Police said they suspected a shadowy racist guerrilla group was behind the latest letter bomb, which exploded on Monday without causing injury.
"The government condemns this latest attack in the strongest possible terms," Vranitzky told reporters after a weekly cabinet meeting. "It will not shake our commitment to democracy."
The letter bomb was addressed to the widowed step-mother of Interior Minister Caspar Einem, a senior member of Vranitzky's ruling Social Democratic Party.

Bomb squad police chief Robert Sturm said the bomb bore all the hallmarks of the Bajuwarian Liberation Army (BLA), which has claimed responsibility for five series of letter bomb attacks since it began its campaign in December 1993.
The group also said it planted a booby-trapped bomb which killed four gypsy men in southeast Austria last year.
"The bomb that exploded on Monday, addressed to Lotte Ingrisch, seems without doubt to have come from the Bajuwarian Liberation Army," Sturm told Austrian radio.
Many of the packages have been intercepted by police but more than half have exploded, injuring targeted foreigners or people linked with immigrant causes in Austria and Germany.

One victim, former Vienna mayor Helmut Zilk, who lost three fingers when he opened a letter bomb in December 1993, lambasted the government for failing to give security officials all the latest equipment available to hunt down the bombers.
"The politicians can no longer escape responsibility because they have not provided all the necessary measures which are now available," Zilk, a Social Democrat elder, told Austrian news agency APA.
Some politicians have called on the government to let the security services have more freedom to tap telephones to try and trap suspected bombers, but the proposals foundered.
Senior police officers have been fired or moved to other jobs following criticism of their handling of the bombings. No suspects have been arrested in connection with the attacks.
Two self-confessed neo-Nazis were detained in 1993 on suspicion of being involved in the first wave of bombs, but they were acquitted last year for lack of evidence.
Some officials believe the BLA may consist of a handful of fanatics but Vienna criminal pyschologist Thomas Mueller said it may be just one individual, like the American Unabomber.
It took U.S. law enforcement officials 17 years to arrest suspected Unabomber Theodore Kaczynski, who is alleged to have killed three people and injured 23 in a bombing campaign.
